options.how: Each skill rises as you use it; skill gains are the only source of character XP, and each level grants a perk point plus health, magicka or stamina.
Kills and quests grant XP levels and skill points; past the level cap, Paragon points fill a board of stat nodes while gear affixes add power.
Nothing survives the 22-minute time loop except what you learned; the ship log tracks clues, and progress is knowing where to go and how.

sources.note: Skyrim: skill increases are the only source of character XP
Diablo IV: Paragon board unlocks after the level cap
Outer Wilds: knowledge is the only progression across the loop

options.game: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
options.how: Four shrine Spirit Orbs buy a Heart Container or Stamina Vessel at a Goddess Statue; weapons break, so gear is never lasting power.
Power is gear score: each equipped item has a score and a rarity tier, and higher World Tiers drop higher-score gear with more talents.

sources.note: Breath of the Wild: four Spirit Orbs trade for a Heart Container or Stamina Vessel
The Division 2: gear score from equipped items, capped by World Tier

options.how: The level cap stays at 80 with no new gear tiers; post-cap XP trains account-wide Masteries such as gliding and mounts, plus cosmetics.
A Power level averaged from equipped gear climbs each season; Powerful and Pinnacle drops push it past soft caps toward harder activities.

sources.note: Guild Wars 2: horizontal progression philosophy, Masteries and cosmetics
Destiny 2: Power level, Powerful and Pinnacle gear caps

options.how: Unlockable weapons are mostly sidegrades: each trades a strength for a weakness against the stock weapon, so items add options, not raw power.
Each level up to 99 grants 5 stat points and 1 skill point; with better gear, earlier areas become trivial as the numbers keep climbing.

sources.note: Team Fortress 2: unlockable weapons with stated upsides and downsides versus stock
Diablo II: stat and skill points per level, level 99 cap

options.how: Coins unlock kart bodies, tires and gliders whose stats trade off (speed against acceleration, weight against handling): new setups, not more power.
Race and outrun wins unlock staged engine, turbo and drivetrain packages; each stage raises the car's power, measured on the dyno.

sources.note: Mario Kart 8: part stats raise some values and lower others
Need for Speed: Underground 2: staged performance parts and dyno

options.how: Upgrading a card is purely cosmetic; it raises Collection Level, which unlocks new cards, so progress widens deck options without stat gains.
Cards level up with copies and gold; a higher-level card has more hitpoints and damage than the same card at a lower level.

sources.note: Marvel Snap: card upgrades raise Collection Level, no stat change
Clash Royale: higher-level cards have more hitpoints and damage

options.how: Beating each Robot Master grants its weapon with limited energy; Mega Man never levels up, so progress is a wider kit of situational tools.
Monsters give XP; each level raises the hero's stats and teaches spells, and grinding levels is the main answer to stronger foes.

sources.note: Mega Man 2: Robot Master weapons with limited energy
Dragon Quest: XP thresholds raise level and stats

options.how: Every car has the same stats on one of six hitbox shapes; unlocks are cosmetic, so progress adds style and choice, never speed.
Prize money buys tuning parts that raise power and handling, and license tests open faster race series as the garage grows stronger.

sources.note: Rocket League: all cars share stats, six hitbox types
Gran Turismo: licenses unlock races, tuning upgrades power and handling

options.how: Darkness gathered in runs buys permanent Mirror of Night talents such as Death Defiance; Chthonic Keys unlock more of them.
Every run starts with the same 4 hearts, bombs and ropes; nothing boosts power, and progress is player skill plus Terra Tunnel shortcuts.

sources.note: Hades: Mirror of Night permanent upgrades bought with Darkness
Spelunky 2: Terra Tunnel shortcuts as the persistent progress

options.how: Cells banked from kills are spent at the Collector on permanent unlocks: extra health flask charges, gold kept on death and new blueprints.
Each death restarts the well with no upgrades kept; the only unlocks are palettes and styles that change starting rules, not power.

sources.note: Dead Cells: Cells spent at the Collector on permanent upgrades
Downwell: styles are the only permanent unlockables

options.how: Gold kept after death buys PowerUps such as Might and Armor that apply to every character in later runs, and can be refunded.
Each run is a total reset with no passive upgrades; milestones unlock new jokers, decks and vouchers that add options, not power.

sources.note: Vampire Survivors: permanent gold-bought PowerUps
Balatro: every run is a total reset, unlocks add new cards

options.how: Heirlooms from expeditions permanently upgrade hamlet buildings, so even a failed run makes later heroes cheaper to heal, train and equip.
Perks, wands and items reset every run with no talent tree; only spell unlocks persist, which add spells to the pool rather than power.

sources.note: Darkest Dungeon: heirlooms upgrade hamlet buildings
Noita: no meta progression or talent tree
Noita: spells with unlock conditions

options.how: All classes share one huge passive tree from different start points, and skill gems socket into any gear, so any class can use any skill.
Each hero has a fixed kit of weapon, abilities and ultimate; you change role by switching heroes mid-match, not by building one.

sources.note: Path of Exile: all classes use the same tree, starting in different places
Overwatch 2: heroes grouped into roles with set abilities

options.how: Combine any two class masteries into one character and mix their skills, then layer Devotion constellations and item-granted skills.
Four dwarf classes each own a fixed loadout, like the Scout's grappling hook or the Driller's drills; upgrades tune gear, not the role.

sources.note: Grim Dawn: combine any of the classes, Devotion and item skills
Deep Rock Galactic: each dwarf has a unique loadout

options.how: Leveled lists pick creatures and container loot by your level, so bandits gain better armor as you level and early areas keep pace.
Enemy stats are set by location, not your level: Limgrave stays gentle and Caelid stays deadly, so you level up or go elsewhere.

sources.note: Oblivion: leveled lists for creatures and items keyed to player level
Elden Ring: enemy difficulty fixed by area

options.how: Colored blocks and doors need a specific power: Morph Ball tunnels, Grapple Beam blocks, Power Bomb walls, so each new ability opens routes.
Every location is reachable from the start; what opens the way is learning a timing, a route or a rule from clues across loops.

sources.note: Metroid Dread: block and door types tied to specific abilities
Outer Wilds: knowledge as the only gate

options.how: Every dungeon and trial lists a required level, such as Sastasha at 15 or Qarn at 35, so content opens only once you are strong enough.
Chapters open areas in a fixed story order; once a section is cleared you usually cannot return, so the plot alone moves you on.

sources.note: Final Fantasy XIV: official duty list with a required level for each dungeon and trial
The Last of Us: chapters played in a fixed order; sections cannot be returned to once passed

options.how: Relics such as Bat form, double jump and Mist form let Alucard reach ledges and pass grates, opening new parts of the castle.
Many secrets need no new item, only decoding the alphabet, number and tetromino codes the world slowly teaches you to read.

sources.note: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night: relics open new areas
Fez: secrets and codes hidden in the world

options.how: Each skill is trained by repeating its own activity, like cutting trees for Woodcutting, and levels to 99 apart from the others.
One XP pool from defeated monsters raises a single character level, and each level lifts every stat at once along a set curve.

sources.note: Old School RuneScape: skills trained by repeating actions, cap 99
Dragon Quest: XP from monsters raises level and stats

options.how: Diamonds gathered in runs unlock permanent upgrades and better equipment, so each attempt makes the next descent a little easier.
No upgrade survives death: you restart the well from the top, and the only permanent unlocks are palettes and starting styles.

sources.note: Crypt of the NecroDancer: diamonds unlock permanent upgrades
Downwell: upgrades are per run, styles are the permanent unlocks

options.how: Each death restarts the cycle, but alien tech such as traversal tools stays unlocked, opening routes and upgrades in later cycles.
Every run starts with fresh wands and perks and no talent tree; only unlocked spells carry over, widening the pool, not your power.

sources.note: Returnal: alien tech upgrades enhance abilities in future cycles
Noita: no meta progression to speak of

options.how: No classes: each level grants a point for a SPECIAL rank or any perk whose SPECIAL requirement you meet, so builds mix freely.
Each deck belongs to one class whose class cards and Hero Power only it can use; neutral cards are shared, but the class kit is set.

sources.note: Fallout 4: one perk point per level, perks gated only by SPECIAL
Hearthstone: class cards and Hero Powers tied to class, neutral cards for all

options.how: Materia slotted into weapons and armor grants spells, commands and summons, and any party member can equip any materia.
You pick four classes such as Fighter or Black Mage at the start; each keeps its own spells and gear all game, upgrading once.

sources.note: Final Fantasy VII: Materia customization
Final Fantasy: four classes chosen at the start, one class change

options.how: No classes or levels: any skill rises through use under a total skill cap, so a fighter can also be a tailor or a mage.
The class picked at creation sets your spells and abilities for good: a Cleric heals, a Warrior tanks, and roles never change.

sources.note: Ultima Online: skill-based characters without classes
EverQuest: class chosen at character creation

options.how: Classes are only starting presets with three skills; any character learns more from skill books and points in any combat ability.
Every hero of a class shares the same stats and skill list, equips four of those skills and never changes class; many trinkets are class-locked.

sources.note: Divinity: Original Sin 2: a class is a build preset with 3 starting skills; skills learned from books, skill points and equipment
Darkest Dungeon: every hero of a class has the same base stats and skills; up to four combat skills equipped; class-specific trinkets

options.how: Every area has a fixed monster level; outleveled zones cut experience through a level-gap penalty, pushing players on to areas that match them.
At launch, open-world monsters scaled to each player's level above a zone's minimum floor, so regions could be tackled in any order.

sources.note: Path of Exile: experience penalty outside a safe range around the area's monster level
Diablo IV: level scaling explained; monsters scale to the player with zone level floors
Diablo IV: monster level scaling described by Blizzard

options.how: Scaling is compressed so most creatures keep set strength by region; deathclaws and cazadores in the north warn new players onto the southern road.
Encounter zones lock creature and loot levels to yours when first entered, so enemies and their gear grow alongside the player.

sources.note: Fallout: New Vegas: Josh Sawyer on deathclaws and cazadores as a warning; less scaling than Fallout 3
Fallout 3: level scaling contrasted with New Vegas's compressed scaling range

options.how: Wild Pokemon and trainers on each route have set levels, so grinding makes earlier routes trivial and later gyms beatable.
Most enemy levels track the party level, so grinding XP buys little; power comes from junctioning drawn magic to stats instead.

sources.note: Pokemon Red and Blue: each route lists fixed wild level ranges and fixed trainer levels
Final Fantasy VIII: enemy stats and abilities scale with the party's level, so grinding is counterproductive
Final Fantasy VIII: enemy level tied to the party's level

options.how: Withers resets a character to level 1 for 100 gold, rebuilding class, ability scores, spells and feats as often as you can pay.
The four attributes set at creation fix every skill's floor and cap for the whole game, so the starting build shapes each check.

sources.note: Baldur's Gate 3: Withers respecs for 100 gold, as often as desired; class, ability scores, spells and feats
Disco Elysium: attributes and skills system
Disco Elysium: starting attribute points set each skill's floor, and its cap is double that

options.how: Out of combat you can swap specializations and traits at any time for free, so one character rebuilds for each encounter.
Activated Sphere Grid nodes stay activated with no refund, so each character's path across the grid is a lasting commitment.

sources.note: Guild Wars 2: traits changed freely out of combat
Final Fantasy X: Sphere Grid activation

options.how: Equipping another class's weapon switches the character to that class and its skills, so one character can level every role.
Each character gets only three breakthrough points for the whole playthrough, and top-tier passives need that tree's breakthrough.

sources.note: Final Fantasy XIV: Armoury System, change class by changing the weapon you hold
Outward: three breakthrough points per character, no way to gain more
Outward: tier 3 passives require the tree's breakthrough

options.how: Quick-Change stations reset every skill point for a small fee, so skill trees can be rebuilt whenever the build stops working.
Each canister offers a choice of two augmentations for one slot; installing one forfeits the other, and installed augs cannot be removed.

sources.note: Borderlands 2: Quick-Change stations clear spent skill points for a small fee
Deus Ex: each canister holds two augmentations, only one can be installed; installations are permanent

options.how: Skills stop at level 99; XP keeps counting to 200 million for rankings, but no further levels or power come from it.
Ascension resets the run for Hero Souls that grant permanent power, and zones go on without end, so the climb never stops.

sources.note: Old School RuneScape: level 99 cap, 200m XP cap
Clicker Heroes: ascension for Hero Souls, endless zones

options.how: Character level stops at 99; a maxed hero grows only through better gear, with no further levels or points to chase.
Characters level to 9999, then Transmigration restarts them at level 1 with stronger growth per level, a loop you can repeat.

sources.note: Diablo II: experience table ends at level 99
Disgaea: max level 9999 and Transmigration

options.how: Level 80 has stayed the cap since launch; past it, XP trains Masteries, and no expansion raised the level or the gear tier.
Ascending resets the bakery for prestige levels worth +1% production each and heavenly chips for upgrades, again and again.

sources.note: Guild Wars 2: level 80 cap with horizontal progression
Cookie Clicker: ascension, prestige and heavenly chips

options.how: Mario and Luigi level up through battles to a hard cap of 100, so growth ends and the late game tests the build you have.
Ascending resets the bakery for prestige levels and heavenly chips that buy permanent upgrades, a loop meant to repeat again and again.

sources.note: Mario & Luigi: Brothership: maximum level 100
Cookie Clicker: ascension resets the run for prestige and heavenly chips; achievements for 10, 100 and 1,000 ascensions

options.how: Paying Withers 100 gold returns a character to level 1 to rebuild class, ability scores, spells and feats, as often as you like.
Spent skill points can never be refunded; with no level cap the answer to a bad pick is to level further, not to rebuild.

sources.note: Baldur's Gate 3: Withers respecs for 100 gold, as often as desired
Starfield: you cannot reset skill points
